name: Femi Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the packing hall of an online clothes shop's warehouse, on the industrial estate past the football ground. I'm on days, seven till half three, thirty hours guaranteed. Most of the day I take picked items off the conveyor, fold them, bag them, print the label and send them down the line. Two days a week I'm on returns, opening bags of stuff people sent back and deciding if it can be sold again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Returns wear me out, honestly, because you never know what's in the bag, and I'm still slow at grading the clothes. What I like is the music on the packing bench and the lads on my line, Tomasz and Dev. My girlfriend Ines does home care visits, so we compare sore feet at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, it was mostly marketing. At work I'd joke that the robot revolution turned out to be a better label printer. I'd probably share a meme about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays a job, which is fine by me. But it doesn't fix the money. I'm on the lower rate because I'm still new, and the rent keeps creeping up whether AI is clever or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the packing and ask my team leader, Sandra, for more returns shifts, because they pay a bit more once you're graded. I'd use the AI chatbot now and then like I already do, to write letters to the landlord. And I'd try to put 40 a month aside in a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal. A bit flat, like the weather staying grey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thirty hours guaranteed. Is that enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. Ines and I split everything, and after rent and the bus passes there's maybe 100 left at the end of the month. One broken phone and we're eating pasta for three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the hall after Christmas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They let the agency people go in January and the hall goes quiet. I'm permanent, so I'm safe, but my overtime disappears. That's when the money really pinches.

say: AI was mostly **marketing**, and the big revolution turned out to be a better **label printer**.
I'd share a meme about it at work and online, then move on.
think: My **job stays a job**, which is fine, but it doesn't fix the money.
I'm on the **lower rate** while still new, and rent keeps creeping up regardless.
do: Ask Sandra for more **returns shifts**, which pay a bit more once graded.
Put **40 a month** into a separate account.
Keep using the **AI chatbot** now and then for landlord letters.
feel: **Normal**, a bit flat, like grey weather that never quite clears.
S0.quote: One broken phone and we're eating pasta for three weeks.
fieldNote: His job feels **secure** here, but there's only about 100 left at month end.
**January** is the pinch, when overtime vanishes after the Christmas peak.
He's relaxed about AI, using a **chatbot** for letters without thinking twice.

steps.text: Ask Sandra for more returns shifts once graded
Move 40 a month into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to get organised and a bad time to be a temp. At work I'd tell the agency lads to grab any permanent contract they're offered. Online I'd probably back whoever's talking about training money for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Packing a jumper into a bag is still hands, so I'm not first in line. But returns is half judging and half typing notes, and that's the kind of thing a camera and a computer could do. If returns goes to software, I lose my better-paid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick with packing and wait to see what works for the first people who try the new systems. If the company offered training on the new returns screens, I'd take it. I'd also join the union, which I've been meaning to do for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the bus is late and you start doing sums about whether you'll lose the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything on returns already changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse is trialling a scanner that photographs the returned item and suggests a grade. Helpers have a way of becoming the boss. Sandra says it's only a helper, but she said that about the label printer too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, this would push me over. Ines is in a union for care workers and she says it's the only reason she gets mileage paid. I'd sign up the week the changes are announced.

say: It's a good time to **get organised** and a bad time to be a temp.
I'd back anyone talking about **training money** for warehouse workers.
think: Packing is still hands, but **returns** is half judging and half typing notes.
If software grades returns, I lose my **better-paid days**.
do: Take any **company training** on the new returns screens.
Join the **union** the week the changes are announced.
Keep packing and watch how the **first users** get on.
feel: **Uneasy**, like doing sums at a late bus stop.
S1.quote: The warehouse is trialling a scanner that photographs the returned item and suggests a grade. Helpers have a way of becoming the boss.
fieldNote: He splits his job sharply: **packing** feels safe, **returns** feels exposed.
A grading **scanner** is already being trialled, which makes the threat concrete.
Joining the **union** is something he'd do once change is proven, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Sign up for company training on the new returns grading screens
Join the warehouse union the week changes are announced
Keep packing and watch how early users of new systems fare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, and fast. Free training, money while you learn, rules on how quickly firms can sack people. I'd be posting that every day, and I'd go on the march if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in real trouble. I left school before finishing, I'm slow on the line, and there are only a couple of warehouses near us. By 2031 packing goes too, and I'd have nothing to show a new boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three years I'd try to get something that robots come to last, like a forklift ticket or electrics. I'd ask the union to push the company to pay for it. Ines and I would stop the gym, drop the streaming and sell my old games console to build up a month of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground has a crack running towards my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the thinking side changes in 2028 and the robots come about 2031. What's your plan for those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use them. That's the one bit of luck, the robots are behind. I'd try to get onto a course in the evenings while I still have a wage, even if it's slow and I'm knackered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Ines that her care job is probably safer than mine, because people want a person when they're old and frail. Then I'd say we need to stop pretending we'll be fine and start planning.

say: The **government** must step in fast with free training and **money while learning**.
I'd post about it daily and join a **march** if one happened.
think: I'd be in **real trouble**: no diploma, slow on the line, few warehouses nearby.
By **2031** packing goes too, and I'd have nothing to show a new boss.
do: Start an **evening course**, like a forklift ticket or electrics, while still earning.
Ask the union to push the company to **pay for training**.
Cancel the gym and streaming, and **sell my console** for a cushion.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a crack running towards my feet.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend Ines that her care job is probably safer than mine, because people want a person when they're old and frail.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year robot gap** as his one piece of luck and wants to study during it.
His **partner's care work** becomes the household's anchor in his eyes.
He wants **public support** and would march, but also takes personal steps.

steps.text: Start an evening forklift or electrics course while still earning
Ask the union to push the company to fund training
Cancel the gym and streaming, and sell his old games console
Join marches calling for free training and pay while learning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Similar message, a bit calmer. I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not waste them arguing about whether it's real. I'd push friends to get on courses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad for me, just not tomorrow. Five years for the office side and eight for the robots means I'd be 35 when packing goes. That's young enough to change, if I'm not still broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence in the first year, then look at an electrical course after that. I'd save 50 a month and not touch it. I'd also start trying the AI tools properly, because by then they'll be in everything and I'd better understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of a plan. Like a long queue, but you can see the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually go to the course on a wet Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hardly anything, honestly. Ines would, she'd kick me out the door. Maybe going with Dev from my line, if he signed up too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you quit packing early to study full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd keep the job as long as it lasts, because we can't live on Ines's wage alone. I'm not jumping before the boat is sinking.

say: We have a **few years**, so don't waste them arguing whether it's real.
I'd push my friends to get onto **courses now**.
think: I'd be **35** when packing goes, young enough to change if not broke.
It's still **bad for me**, just not tomorrow.

Save **50 a month** and leave it untouched.
Start using **AI tools** properly to understand them.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan, like a long queue where I can see the front.
S3.quote: Five years for the office side and eight for the robots means I'd be 35 when packing goes.
fieldNote: He does the **arithmetic** himself, counting the robot delay into his own timeline.

He won't **quit early**, preferring to stay until the job ends.

steps.text: Get a forklift licence in the first year, then an electrical course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually plan, if politicians do their job. I'd keep pushing for training funds, but I wouldn't be shouting so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Packing would carry on for twelve years or so, but my pay would never go up much. The real question is whether I use those years or drift. Knowing me, I'd drift for two of them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd join the union and maybe do the forklift ticket, and save a bit. After a couple of years I'd look at a proper trade, maybe electrician through a part-time apprenticeship. The AI tools I'd pick up as they become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It's far enough that I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your life to look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small flat with Ines that isn't damp, and me doing something where I fix stuff instead of packing it. Kids eventually, but not while I'm on this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you do this year, if this was the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Join the union and stop eating out twice a week. I'd also ask Sandra if the company ever pays for forklift training, because I've never actually asked.

say: This is the version where we can **plan**, if politicians do their job.
I'd keep pushing for **training funds**, but more quietly.
think: Packing lasts about **twelve years**, but my pay would barely rise.
Knowing me, I'd **drift** for two years before I start.
do: Join the **union** this year and stop eating out twice a week.

feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, far enough away to breathe.
S4.quote: Packing would carry on for twelve years or so, but my pay would never go up much.
fieldNote: He feels **calmer**, but his job still ends and his pay stays low, so it's anxious.

steps.text: Join the union at the clothing warehouse this year
Stop eating out twice a week
Ask Sandra about company-paid forklift training, then an apprenticeship

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 scares me most, because I'd have barely any time and no money to learn something new. What would help is a course I can do in the evenings, paid for, with a bit of money if I have to cut my hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Ines. Everybody talks about my job, but if care workers get squeezed too, we're both done. I'd want somebody to think about couples where both of us are on low pay.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about my job, but if care workers get squeezed too, we're both done.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old packer** at an online clothes warehouse, on a thirty-hour contract with returns two days a week.
He and Ines, a home-care worker, have about **100 left** at month end.
He's **steady**: he'd join the union and train once change looks real, but admits he drifts.
He wants **public training money** and sees the robot delay as his chance to learn a trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with almost no time and no money to learn something new.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid evening course**, with some money if he has to cut hours.
Attention to **low-paid couples** like him and Ines, not just his own job.
